chapters.title: 1. Units, Measurement & Motion
chapters.notes:
### 1.1 Physical quantities (রাশি)
- Scalar (স্কেলার রাশি): only magnitude: mass, length, time, speed, distance, work, energy, power, temperature, density, pressure.
- Vector (ভেক্টর রাশি): magnitude + direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight, torque, electric field.
- Pressure, work, energy and electric current are scalars (current has direction but does not follow vector addition).
### 1.2 SI base units (মৌলিক একক)
| Quantity | SI unit | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Length | metre | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

Small & big units (PYQ favourites)
- Light year = distance light travels in one year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m: a unit of distance , not time.
- Parsec = 3.26 light years (largest unit of distance). Astronomical Unit (AU) = mean Earth-Sun distance ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m.
- Angstrom = 10⁻¹⁰ m; Fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m (nuclear size); Micron = 10⁻⁶ m.
- Nautical mile = 1852 m (sea/air navigation); Knot = speed of 1 nautical mile per hour.
- 1 horsepower = 746 W. 1 kWh (Board of Trade unit) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. 1 calorie = 4.186 J.
- Decibel = loudness of sound. Richter scale = earthquake magnitude. Fathom = depth of sea (6 feet).

### 1.4 Motion (গতি)
- Speed = distance / time (scalar). Velocity = displacement / time (vector). If a body returns to the start, displacement = 0 , average velocity = 0.
- Acceleration (ত্বরণ) = change in velocity / time, unit m/s². Negative acceleration = retardation (মন্দন).
- Uniform circular motion: speed constant but velocity changes (direction changes), so it is accelerated motion .
- Equations: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as.
- Momentum (ভরবেগ) p = mv (kg m/s). Heavier hammer drives a nail deeper: more momentum.
### 1.5 Newton's laws of motion
- First law (law of inertia / জাড্যের সূত্র): a body stays at rest or uniform motion unless an external force acts. Examples: passengers fall back when a bus starts suddenly; dust leaves a carpet when beaten. Mass is the measure of inertia.
- Second law: F = ma (force = rate of change of momentum). Impulse = F × t = change in momentum. A cricketer pulls hands back while catching → more time, less force.
- Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Examples: rocket propulsion , recoil of a gun, swimming, walking.
- Conservation of momentum: total momentum stays constant if no external force acts (rocket, gun recoil).
- Centripetal force acts towards the centre in circular motion; "centrifugal force" is the apparent outward force (used in cream separator, washing-machine dryer).

chapters.title: 2. Gravitation, Work, Energy & Friction
chapters.notes:
### 2.1 Gravitation (মহাকর্ষ)
- Newton's law: F = G m₁ m₂ / r². G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg² (universal constant; value first measured by Henry Cavendish).
- g (acceleration due to gravity) ≈ 9.8 m/s². g is maximum at the poles, minimum at the equator ; it decreases with height and with depth; g = 0 at the centre of the Earth .
- Mass is constant everywhere; weight (W = mg) changes. On the Moon, g is ~1/6 of Earth's, so weight is 1/6.
- Escape velocity of Earth = 11.2 km/s (Moon 2.4 km/s). It does not depend on the mass of the object.
- Orbital velocity near the Earth ≈ 7.9 km/s. Geostationary satellite: height ≈ 36,000 km, period 24 h, moves west to east.
- In a freely falling lift or orbiting satellite, a person feels weightless. If the lift accelerates upward, apparent weight increases.
- Kepler's laws: orbits are elliptical with the Sun at one focus; equal areas in equal times; T² ∝ r³.
### 2.2 Work, energy & power (কার্য, শক্তি, ক্ষমতা)
- Work W = F × s × cos θ (joule). No work if force ⟂ displacement (coolie carrying a load on a level road does zero work against gravity; a satellite in circular orbit).
- Kinetic energy = ½mv²: doubling speed makes KE four times . Potential energy = mgh.
- Power = work / time (watt). 1 HP = 746 W.
- Law of conservation of energy: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted.
| Device | Energy conversion |
|---|---|
| Electric motor / fan | electrical → mechanical |
| Generator / dynamo | mechanical → electrical |
| Battery (cell) | chemical → electrical |
| Solar cell | light → electrical |
| Microphone | sound → electrical |
| Loudspeaker | electrical → sound |
| Device | Energy conversion |
| Electric bulb | electrical → light + heat |
| Steam engine | heat → mechanical |

### 2.3 Friction (ঘর্ষণ)
- Friction opposes relative motion. Order: static > sliding > rolling . That is why wheels and ball bearings are used.
- Reduced by lubricants, polishing, ball bearings, streamlining. Increased by tyre treads, sand on rails, spikes on shoes.
- Walking is possible because of friction; it is difficult to walk on ice (very low friction).
### 2.4 Simple machines & centre of gravity
- Lever classes: class 1 fulcrum in middle (scissors, see-saw, pliers); class 2 load in middle (nutcracker, wheelbarrow, bottle opener); class 3 effort in middle (forceps, tongs, fishing rod, human forearm).
- Stability is more when the centre of gravity is low and the base is wide. Racing cars are low; a man carrying a load on one side leans the other way.

chapters.title: 3. Properties of Matter & Fluids
chapters.notes:
### 3.1 Elasticity (স্থিতিস্থাপকতা)
- Hooke's law (1660): within the elastic limit, stress ∝ strain. Steel is more elastic than rubber (needs more stress for the same strain).
- Young's modulus (length), bulk modulus (volume), modulus of rigidity (shape). Unit = N/m².
### 3.2 Pressure (চাপ)
- Pressure = force / area (pascal). Sharp knife, nails and needles have small area → more pressure.
- Wide straps on bags and broad tyres reduce pressure.
- Liquid pressure = hρg: increases with depth. Dams are thicker at the bottom.
- Atmospheric pressure at sea level ≈ 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 76 cm of mercury. It decreases with height:
- ink leaks from a pen in an aeroplane, nose bleeding at high altitude, cooking is difficult in mountains (boiling point falls). Mercury barometer was invented by Torricelli.
- Pressure cooker: higher pressure → higher boiling point → faster cooking.
### 3.3 Pascal, Archimedes & floating
- Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions. Used in hydraulic lift, hydraulic brake, hydraulic press .
- Archimedes' principle: a body in a fluid loses weight equal to the weight of fluid displaced (buoyancy /প্লবতা).
- Law of floatation: a body floats if its weight = weight of liquid displaced. Iron ship floats (hollow, displaces more water); iron needle sinks.
- Ships float higher in sea water (denser) than in river water. Ice floats because its density is less than water. When floating ice melts, water level stays the same .
- An egg sinks in fresh water but floats in salt water. A swimmer finds it easier to swim in sea water.
### 3.4 Bernoulli, surface tension & viscosity
- Bernoulli's principle: where speed of fluid is high, pressure is low. Lift of aeroplane wings, roofs blown off in storms, atomiser/sprayer, a ball spinning (swing).
- Surface tension (পৃষ্ঠটান): liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane. Drops and bubbles are spherical (minimum surface area); insects walk on water; it decreases with rise in
- temperature and with soap/detergent (hot soapy water cleans better).
- Capillarity (কৈশিকতা): rise of liquid in a thin tube: oil rising in a lamp wick, water rising in plants, ink in blotting paper, towel soaking water. Mercury falls in a capillary.
- Viscosity (সান্দ্রতা): internal friction of a fluid. Honey, glycerine, oil are viscous. Viscosity of liquids decreases on heating ; of gases increases. Lubricant oil grade depends on viscosity.
- Density of water is maximum at 4 °C (anomalous expansion): fish survive under frozen lakes.

chapters.title: 4. Heat & Thermodynamics
chapters.notes:
### 4.1 Heat & temperature (তাপ ও তাপমাত্রা)
- Heat is energy (joule/calorie); temperature is degree of hotness (kelvin). Heat flows from higher to lower temperature.
- Scales: C/100 = (F - 32)/180 = (K - 273)/100. -40 °C = -40 °F . Body temperature 37 °C = 98.6 °F = 310 K. Absolute zero = 0 K = -273.15 °C.
- Clinical thermometer range 35-42 °C (95-110 °F) with a kink. Mercury is used because it is opaque, shiny, does not wet glass and expands uniformly. Mercury thermometer: Fahrenheit. Very high temperature: pyrometer.
- Specific heat of water is very high (4186 J/kg K): water is a good coolant (car radiator); sea breeze and land breeze.
- Latent heat: heat absorbed during change of state without temperature change. Steam at 100 °C burns more than water at 100 °C (latent heat of vaporisation 2260 kJ/kg). Ice: latent heat of fusion 336 kJ/kg.
### 4.2 Transfer of heat (তাপ সঞ্চালন)
| Mode | How | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Conduction (পরিবহণ) | particle to particle, mainly solids | metal spoon gets hot; cooking utensils with wooden handles |
| Convection (পরিচলন) | movement of fluid | sea and land breeze, car radiator cooling , ventilators near roof |
| Radiation (বিকিরণ) | no medium needed | Sun's heat reaching Earth; fastest mode |

- Thermos flask prevents all three (vacuum stops conduction and convection, silvered walls stop radiation).
- Black surfaces absorb and emit more heat; white reflects. Light-coloured clothes in summer.
- Silver is the best conductor of heat and electricity; then copper, aluminium.
### 4.3 Expansion & changes of state
- Gaps left in railway tracks; telephone wires sag in summer. Water expands on freezing: pipes burst in winter.
- Evaporation causes cooling (earthen pot, sweating). Faster with high temperature, wind, larger surface area, low humidity.
- Boiling point rises with pressure and with impurities (salt); melting point of ice falls with pressure (regelation) and with impurities (ice + salt = freezing mixture).
- Sublimation: solid → gas directly (camphor, naphthalene, dry ice, iodine).
- Dew point; relative humidity measured by hygrometer.
### 4.4 Gas laws & thermodynamics
- Boyle's law: PV = constant (constant T). Charles's law: V ∝ T (constant P). Graham's law: rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√density.
- First law of thermodynamics = conservation of energy (ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW).
- Second law: heat cannot flow by itself from cold to hot body; no engine is 100% efficient.
- Refrigerator transfers heat from inside to outside using work.
- Keeping a fridge door open warms the room (more heat is released than removed).
- Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling ∝ temperature difference.

chapters.title: 5. Waves & Sound
chapters.notes:
### 5.1 Waves (তরঙ্গ)
- Transverse wave: particles vibrate ⟂ to direction (light, waves on string). Longitudinal wave:
- particles vibrate along direction, with compressions and rarefactions ( sound in air ).
- v = f λ (speed = frequency × wavelength). Frequency in hertz; period T = 1/f.
- Mechanical waves need a medium (sound); electromagnetic waves do not (light, radio).
### 5.2 Sound (শব্দ)
- Sound cannot travel in vacuum (astronauts use radio on the Moon).
- Speed of sound: air ≈ 332 m/s at 0 °C (≈ 343 at 20 °C), water ≈ 1480 m/s, steel ≈ 5000 m/s. Order:
- solid > liquid > gas .
- Speed of sound increases with temperature and humidity; not affected by pressure change at constant temperature.
- Audible range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz = infrasonic (earthquakes, elephants, whales).
- Above 20 kHz = ultrasonic (bats, dolphins; SONAR, ultrasound scan, cleaning, kidney stones).
- Pitch depends on frequency (women's voice has higher pitch); loudness on amplitude (decibel);
- quality /timbre on waveform (overtones).
- Noise above ~80 dB is harmful; > 120 dB painful.
### 5.3 Echo, resonance & Doppler effect
- Echo: reflected sound heard separately; persistence of hearing 0.1 s, so minimum distance ≈ 17 m . Reverberation: persistence of sound by many reflections (auditoriums use sound absorbing materials).
- SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) uses ultrasound to find depth of sea. Bats navigate by echolocation.
- Resonance: forced frequency equals natural frequency → large amplitude. Soldiers break step while crossing a bridge. Tuning a radio is resonance.
- Doppler effect: apparent change in frequency due to relative motion: pitch of a train whistle rises when approaching. Used in radar speed guns, red-shift of galaxies.
- Sonic boom: shock wave of a supersonic jet. Mach number = speed of object / speed of sound.

chapters.title: 6. Light & Optics
chapters.notes:
### 6.1 Nature of light
- Light is an electromagnetic wave (transverse); speed in vacuum ≈ 3 × 10 ⁸ m/s . Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
- Wave nature: interference, diffraction, polarisation. Particle nature: photoelectric effect (photon, Planck /Einstein). Wave nature of matter: de Broglie.
- Visible spectrum (VIBGYOR): violet has shortest wavelength, highest frequency, deviates most ;
- red has longest wavelength, deviates least (used in danger signals because it scatters least).
### 6.2 Reflection & mirrors (প্রতিফলন)
- Angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Plane mirror: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted image. Two mirrors at angle θ give (360/θ - 1) images.
- Concave mirror: shaving / dentist's mirror, headlights, torch, solar cookers, reflecting telescopes.
- Convex mirror: rear-view mirror of vehicles (wide field, erect, small image), street lights.
- Focal length f = R/2.
### 6.3 Refraction (প্রতিসরণ)
- Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another. Refractive index n = c / v. Diamond n ≈ 2.42 (very high), water 1.33, glass 1.5.
- Examples: stick looks bent in water; pond looks shallower; stars twinkle (atmospheric refraction);
- Sun seen 2 min before sunrise and after sunset.
- Total internal reflection: light from denser to rarer medium beyond critical angle. Sparkling of diamond, optical fibre, mirage .
- Dispersion: white light splits into colours by a prism (first shown by Newton). Rainbow = dispersion + refraction + total internal reflection in raindrops; seen opposite the Sun.
- Scattering: blue sky (blue scatters more, Rayleigh), red sunrise/sunset, white clouds. Sky looks black to astronauts . Raman effect (C.V. Raman, 1928; Nobel 1930) = scattering of light; 28 Feb = National Science Day.
### 6.4 Lenses & the eye
- Convex lens (converging): magnifying glass, camera, projector, spectacles for hypermetropia.
- Concave lens (diverging): myopia spectacles.
- Power P = 1/f (metre); unit dioptre. Convex = +, concave = -.
| Defect | Cannot see | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Myopia (short sight, হ্রস্বদৃষ্টি) | far objects | concave lens |
| Hypermetropia (long sight, দীর্ঘদৃষ্টি) | near objects | convex lens |
| Presbyopia (old age) | near objects | bifocal lens |
| Astigmatism | uneven focus | cylindrical lens |

- Image on the retina is real and inverted . Least distance of distinct vision = 25 cm. Persistence of vision ≈ 1/16 s (cinema works on this).
- Primary colours of light: red, green, blue. Red + green = yellow; red + blue = magenta; green + blue = cyan; all three = white.
- A red rose looks black in green light (it absorbs green).

chapters.title: 7. Electricity & Magnetism
chapters.notes:
### 7.1 Electric current (তড়িৎ প্রবাহ)
- Current I = Q / t (ampere). Flow of electrons is opposite to conventional current. Net charge in a current- carrying conductor is zero .
- Ohm's law (G.S. Ohm, 1827): V = IR at constant temperature. Resistance R = ρL/A: ∝ length, ∝ 1/area.
- Resistance of metals increases with temperature; of semiconductors decreases . Superconductor:
- resistance becomes zero (Kamerlingh Onnes, 1911).
- Series: R = R₁ + R₂ (same current). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (same voltage). Domestic wiring is parallel , so each appliance gets 220 V and can be switched separately.
- Kirchhoff's laws: junction law (sum of incoming = outgoing currents) and loop law (energy conservation).
- Silver is the best conductor; copper is used in wires (cheap). Human body resistance ≈ 10⁵-10⁶ Ω (dry skin).
### 7.2 Heating effect & domestic electricity
- Joule's law: H = I²Rt. Used in heater, iron, bulb, fuse .
- Fuse wire: high resistance and low melting point (tin-lead alloy); connected in series in the live wire. MCB trips automatically on overcurrent.
- Heater element: nichrome (high resistance, high melting point). Bulb filament: tungsten (melting point ≈ 3400 °C); bulbs filled with inert nitrogen/argon to increase filament life.
- India: AC supply 220-230 V, 50 Hz . Wires: live (brown/red), neutral (light blue/black), earth (green). The longest, thickest pin of a 3-pin plug is earth .
- Electric energy = power × time; 1 unit = 1 kWh. Example: a 100 W bulb for 10 hours = 1 unit.
- Lightning conductor protects buildings (Benjamin Franklin showed lightning is electric).
### 7.3 Cells & electrostatics
- Electric cell: chemical → electrical. Volta made the first battery (1800). Dry cell (Leclanché) ≈ 1.5 V; lead-acid battery in cars (rechargeable); Li-ion in mobiles. In a cell symbol, the long thin line is +, the short thick line is -.
- Capacitor stores charge (unit farad). Electroscope detects charge. Charge on a hollow conductor stays on the outer surface: no electric field inside (safe inside a car during lightning).
- Electroplating: depositing a metal layer by electrolysis (Faraday's laws).
### 7.4 Magnetism & electromagnetism (চুম্বক ও তড়িৎ-চুম্বক)
- Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; repulsion is the sure test of magnetism. A freely suspended magnet points north-south.
- Magnetic materials: ferromagnetic (iron, cobalt, nickel), paramagnetic (aluminium), diamagnetic (bismuth, copper, water). Soft iron is used in electromagnets (easily magnetised and demagnetised); steel for permanent magnets.
- Above the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet loses its magnetism.
- Oersted (1820): current produces a magnetic field (compass deflects). Faraday: electromagnetic induction: changing magnetic flux induces current → generator, transformer, induction cooker .
- Fleming's left-hand rule: motor. Right-hand rule: generator. Lenz's law: induced current opposes its cause.
- Transformer steps up or steps down AC voltage only (does not work on DC); does not change frequency. Power is transmitted at high voltage to reduce loss.
- Galvanometer detects current; with low shunt resistance → ammeter; with high series resistance → voltmeter.
- AC to DC: rectifier; DC to AC: inverter. Dynamo / AC generator: mechanical → electrical. Earth's magnetic field: magnetic declination and dip.

chapters.notes:
### 8.1 Atom (পরমাণু)
| Particle | Discovered by | Charge |

- Bohr model (1913): electrons in fixed orbits. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Isotopes: same atomic number, different mass number; isobars: same mass number.
### 8.2 Radioactivity (তেজস্ক্রিয়তা)
- Discovered by Henri Becquerel (1896) in uranium; Marie & Pierre Curie discovered polonium and radium.
| Ray | Nature | Penetrating power |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (α) | helium nucleus, +2 charge | least; most ionising |
| Beta (β) | fast electrons | medium |
| Gamma (γ) | electromagnetic wave, no charge | highest |

- Half-life: time for half the nuclei to decay. Unit of radioactivity: becquerel (SI), curie. Radioactivity is not affected by temperature or pressure .
- Uses: cobalt-60 (cancer treatment), iodine-131 (thyroid), carbon-14 (dating of fossils), uranium- 235 (fuel).
- Nuclear fission (heavy nucleus splits; atom bomb, nuclear reactor; Fermi built the first reactor, 1942). Fusion (light nuclei join; Sun's energy, hydrogen bomb). E = mc² (Einstein).

- Piezoelectric effect: quartz crystal in watches. Photoelectric effect (Hertz 1887; explained by Einstein, Nobel 1921).
- EM spectrum (increasing frequency): radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays.
- Uses: infrared (TV remote, night vision, heating), UV (sterilisation; ozone absorbs it), microwave (oven, radar), X-rays (Roentgen, 1895; bone imaging).

chapters.title: 9. Matter, Atomic Structure & Mole Concept
chapters.notes:
### 9.1 States of matter (পদার্থের অবস্থা)
- Matter has mass and occupies space; it can neither be created nor destroyed (law of conservation of mass, Lavoisier).
- Three common states: solid, liquid, gas. Plasma = ionised gas, the fourth state (identified by William Crookes, 1879); found in the Sun, stars, lightning, neon signs.
- Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) = fifth state at near absolute zero (predicted by S.N. Bose and Einstein, 1924-25; made in 1995).
- Superfluid: liquid at very low temperature that flows without viscosity, can climb up walls (liquid helium).
- Diffusion is fastest in gases. Sublimation: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, dry ice (solid CO₂).
### 9.2 Mixtures & separation
| Method | Used to separate |
|---|---|
| Distillation | liquids with different boiling points; pure water from salt water |
| Fractional distillation | crude petroleum; liquid air (N₂, O₂) |
| Sublimation | camphor / ammonium chloride from salt |
| Chromatography | colours of ink, pigments |
| Centrifugation | cream from milk |
| Crystallisation | pure salt / sugar from solution |
| Separating funnel | immiscible liquids (oil and water) |

### 9.3 Atom & sub-atomic particles
- Dalton (1808): atomic theory. J.J. Thomson: electron (1897), plum-pudding model. Rutherford (1911): nucleus. Bohr (1913): fixed orbits. Chadwick (1932): neutron.
- Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. Ordinary hydrogen (protium) has no neutron .
| Term | Same | Different | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Isotopes | atomic number | mass number | 1 H, 2H (deuterium), ³H (tritium); C-12, C-14 |
| Isobars | mass number | atomic number | 40 Ar and 40Ca |
| Isotones | number of neutrons | protons | 31 P and 32S (16 neutrons each) |

- Uses of isotopes: iodine-131 (thyroid / goitre & thyroid cancer), cobalt-60 (cancer), carbon-14 (age of fossils), uranium-235 (nuclear fuel), phosphorus-32 (agriculture research).
- Heavy water = D₂O (moderator in reactors).
### 9.4 Mole, valency & laws
- Avogadro number N = 6.022 × 10 ²³ particles per mole. 1 mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 litres.
- Valency: combining capacity of an element, measured by the number of hydrogen atoms it combines with or replaces. Noble gases: valency zero.
- Ideal gas obeys Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws (H₂, N₂ come close).
- Physical change (reversible, no new substance): melting of ice, dissolving salt, magnetising iron.
- Chemical change (new substance): rusting, burning, curdling of milk, digestion, ripening of fruit.

chapters.title: 10. Periodic Table, Metals & Non-metals
chapters.notes:
### 10.1 Periodic table (পর্যায় সারণি)
- Mendeleev (Russia, 1869): arranged elements by atomic mass . Moseley (1913): modern periodic law based on atomic number .
- Modern table: 18 groups (vertical) and 7 periods (horizontal); 118 elements.
- Group 1 = alkali metals (Li, Na, K); group 2 = alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca); group 17 = halogens (F, Cl, Br, I); group 18 = noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn), valency zero.
- Most electronegative element: fluorine. Most reactive metal in common use: potassium/caesium.
- Lightest element: hydrogen; lightest metal: lithium.
### 10.2 Metals, non-metals & metalloids (ধাতু, অধাতু, ধাতুকল্প)
- Metals: lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors (gold, silver, copper, iron). Most malleable and ductile: gold. Best conductor: silver.
- Non-metals: brittle, poor conductors (carbon, sulphur, phosphorus, oxygen, chlorine). Exception:
- graphite conducts electricity .
- Metalloids (ধাতুকল্প): show both properties: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony.
- Liquids at room temperature: mercury (metal) and bromine (non-metal) . Gallium and caesium melt near body temperature.
- Sodium and potassium are stored in kerosene (react violently with air and water); sodium is lighter than water. White phosphorus is stored under water.
- Hydrogen is a non-metal but is placed in group 1 (forms H⁺ like metals).
- Most abundant element in the Earth's crust: oxygen, then silicon; most abundant metal:
- aluminium. Most abundant gas in air: nitrogen (78%). Most abundant element in the universe:
- hydrogen.
### 10.3 Corrosion & protection (ক্ষয়)
- Rust = hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Needs both oxygen and moisture ; faster in salty water.
- Prevention: painting, oiling, galvanisation (coating iron with zinc ), electroplating, tinning (tin cans), making stainless steel.
- Silver turns black (Ag₂S, with H₂S); copper turns green (basic copper carbonate).
- Amphoteric oxides (react with both acids and bases): ZnO, Al₂O₃.
### 10.4 Important gases
| Gas | Key fact |
|---|---|
| Hydrogen | lightest; burns with a pop sound; used in hydrogenation of oils (vanaspati), fuel cells |
| Oxygen | supports burning; isolated by Priestley (1774) and Scheele; ozone O₃ protects from UV |
| Nitrogen | 78% of air; used in food packing (chips) to prevent oxidation, fertilisers via ammonia |
| Carbon dioxide | fire extinguisher, soda water, dry ice; main greenhouse gas |
| Carbon monoxide | poisonous, forms carboxyhaemoglobin; from incomplete burning |
| Helium | in weather balloons, with O₂ for deep-sea divers |
| Neon | red advertising signs |
| Argon | filled in electric bulbs |
| Chlorine | bleaching, disinfecting water |
| Ammonia | pungent smell; Haber process; fertilisers, refrigerant |
| Hydrogen sulphide | rotten-egg smell |

chapters.title: 11. Acids, Bases, Salts & Chemical Reactions
chapters.notes:
### 11.1 Acids & bases (অম্ল ও ক্ষার)
- Arrhenius: acid gives H⁺ in water; base gives OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry (1923): acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor.
- Acids: sour, turn blue litmus red . Bases: bitter, soapy, turn red litmus blue . Phenolphthalein turns pink in bases; methyl orange red in acid.
- Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
- Amphoteric / amphiprotic: acts as acid and base (water, ZnO, Al₂O₃).
- Antacids (for acidity) are mild bases: milk of magnesia Mg(OH)₂, sodium bicarbonate, aluminium hydroxide.
### 11.2 pH scale
- pH = -log[H⁺]; scale 0-14 (Sørensen). pH 7 neutral, < 7 acidic, > 7 basic.
| Substance | approx. pH |
|---|---|
| Gastric juice (HCl) | 1.0-2.0 |
| Lemon juice | ~2.4 |
| Vinegar | ~3 |
| Acid rain | < 5.6 |
| Pure water | 7 |
| Human blood | 7.35-7.45 (slightly basic) |
| Sea water | ~8 |
| Milk of magnesia | ~10 |

- Tooth decay starts below pH 5.5. Acidic soil is treated with lime (CaO / CaCO₃).
### 11.3 Natural acids (প্রাকৃতিক অম্ল)

- Oleum = H₂S₂O₇ (SO₃ in conc. H₂SO₄). H₂SO₄ = "king of chemicals" (contact process). HNO₃:

- Strong bases: NaOH (caustic soda), KOH (caustic potash). LiOH absorbs CO₂ in submarines and spacecraft.

### 11.5 Chemical reactions
- Oxidation: addition of oxygen / loss of hydrogen / loss of electrons . Reduction: gain of electrons.
- Both together = redox: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O (CuO reduced, H₂ oxidised).
- Types: combination, decomposition, displacement (Zn + CuSO₄), double displacement, neutralisation, combustion.
- Catalyst changes reaction speed without being used up (iron in Haber process, V₂O₅ in contact process, nickel in hydrogenation, enzymes in the body).

chapters.notes:
### 12.1 Terms (পরিভাষা)
- Mineral: naturally occurring compound of a metal. Ore: mineral from which the metal is extracted profitably (all ores are minerals, not all minerals are ores).

chapters.title: 13. Industrial & Everyday Chemistry
chapters.notes:
### 13.1 Water (জল)
- Temporary hardness: bicarbonates of Ca and Mg → removed by boiling or Clark's method (lime).
- Permanent hardness: chlorides and sulphates of Ca and Mg → removed by washing soda, ion exchange (permutit/zeolite).
- Hard water does not lather with soap and forms scale in boilers (important for factories).
- Water is purified by chlorination, bleaching powder, ozone, UV; alum (ফটকিরি) settles mud (coagulation). Fluoride in excess causes fluorosis; arsenic in groundwater (Murshidabad, Nadia, Malda).
### 13.2 Soaps, detergents, glass & cement
- Soap = sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids (sodium stearate); made by saponification (oil/fat + NaOH). Potassium soaps are soft (shaving creams).
- Detergents = sodium salts of sulphonic acids; work in hard water. Non-biodegradable ones cause water pollution (foam, eutrophication with phosphates).
- Glass: fusing sand (SiO₂) + soda ash (Na₂CO₃) + limestone. Glass is a supercooled liquid .
- Pyrex/borosilicate glass resists heat; colours: cobalt oxide = blue, chromium oxide = green, ferrous = green, manganese dioxide = violet, gold chloride = ruby red.
- Portland cement (Joseph Aspdin, 1824): mainly lime CaO (~60-63%), silica SiO₂ (~20-22%), alumina, iron oxide; gypsum is added to slow setting .
### 13.3 Fuels (জ্বালানি)
| Fuel | Main component | Note |
|---|---|---|
| LPG | butane (+ propane) | ethyl mercaptan added for smell to detect leaks |
| CNG | methane | cleaner fuel for vehicles |
| Natural gas / biogas / marsh gas | methane | biogas from cow dung (~55-65% CH₄) |
| Water gas | CO + H₂ | industrial fuel |
| Producer gas | CO + N₂ | low calorific value |
| Coal gas | H₂ + CH₄ + CO |  |

- Coal grades by carbon %: peat < lignite < bituminous < anthracite (best, ~90% C).
- Calorific value: hydrogen has the highest (~150 kJ/g) but is hard to store. Octane number (petrol quality; knocking); cetane number (diesel).
- Fire extinguishers: CO₂ for electrical and oil fires; never use water on oil or electrical fires ; soda-acid type for wood/paper.
### 13.4 Polymers, fertilisers & other chemicals
- Polymers: polythene (ethylene), PVC (vinyl chloride; pipes), Teflon (non-stick), Bakelite (phenol + formaldehyde; switches, thermosetting), nylon (first synthetic fibre), polyester/terylene, natural rubber = polyisoprene.
- Vulcanisation: heating rubber with sulphur to make it hard and elastic (Goodyear). BUNA-S = butadiene + styrene; BUNA-N = butadiene + acrylonitrile; neoprene (chloroprene).
- Fertilisers: urea (46% N, highest nitrogen), ammonium sulphate, superphosphate of lime, NPK, DAP.
- Explosives: TNT (trinitrotoluene), dynamite (nitroglycerine, Alfred Nobel), RDX, gunpowder (KNO₃ + S + charcoal).
- Medicines: aspirin (analgesic), paracetamol (antipyretic), penicillin (antibiotic, Fleming 1928), chloroform & nitrous oxide (anaesthetics), Dettol (antiseptic).
- Food chemicals: sodium benzoate (preservative), monosodium glutamate (flavour), saccharin/aspartame (sweeteners), vanaspati = hydrogenated oil (nickel catalyst).

chapters.title: 14. Carbon & Organic Chemistry
chapters.notes:
### 14.1 Carbon & its allotropes (কার্বনের রূপভেদ)
- Carbon forms the most compounds due to catenation (self-linking) and valency 4.
- Diamond: hardest natural substance, bad conductor, each C bonded to 4 others; high refractive index (2.42). Graphite: soft, layered, good conductor , used as lubricant, pencil "lead", electrodes, moderator.
- Fullerene (C₆₀, buckyball; Kroto, Curl, Smalley, 1985), graphene (single layer), carbon nanotubes.
- Amorphous forms: coal, charcoal, coke, lamp black.
- Activated charcoal adsorbs gases (gas masks, water filters).
### 14.2 Hydrocarbons
| Family | General formula | Bond | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alkane (paraffin) | CnH2n+2 | single | methane CH₄, ethane, propane, butane |
| Alkene (olefin) | CnH2n | double | ethylene C₂H₄ (ripens fruit) |
| Alkyne | CnH2n-2 | triple | acetylene C₂H₂ (oxy-acetylene welding) |

- Benzene (C₆H₆) is aromatic (Kekulé's ring structure). Saturated = single bonds; unsaturated = double/triple bonds.
### 14.3 Functional groups & common compounds
| Group | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Alcohol | -OH | ethanol C₂H₅OH, methanol CH₃OH |
| Aldehyde | -CHO | formaldehyde HCHO (40% solution = formalin) |
| Ketone | >C=O | acetone (nail polish remover) |
| Carboxylic acid | -COOH | acetic acid CH₃COOH |
| Ester | -COOR | fruity smell; perfumes, flavours |
| Amine | -NH₂ | aniline (dyes) |

- Ethanol: in alcoholic drinks; made by fermentation of molasses (yeast enzymes). Rectified spirit = 95.6% ethanol ; absolute alcohol = 100%; denatured spirit = ethanol + methanol/pyridine (unfit to drink).
- Methanol is poisonous: causes blindness and death (hooch tragedies).
- Power alcohol = ethanol blended with petrol (India's E20 target).
- Chloroform CHCl₃ (anaesthetic); CFCs (freon) deplete ozone; DDT (insecticide, banned for farm use).
- Biomolecules: carbohydrates (glucose C₆H₁₂O₆, sucrose = cane sugar, fructose = sweetest natural sugar), proteins (amino acids), fats (glycerol + fatty acids).
